toc.title: Purpose and the principles it serves

html:
1Purpose and the principles it serves

The progress practice gives the project a way to monitor actual results against the plan, to forecast the objectives and continued viability, and to control deviations that are not acceptable. Good control answers three questions at every level: where are we, where will we end up, and what must change?

It serves manage by exception (tolerances and escalation), manage by stages (decision points at stage ends), ensure continued business justification (forecasts show whether the case holds), learn from experience (lessons captured as they appear) and focus on products (progress measured by products delivered, not hours spent).

Exam tip

. Progress is about forecasting, not only reporting. An approach that tells the board where the stage will end is stronger than one that only describes what has happened.

2The key management products

Product What it is for
Daily log (project log) The project manager's informal notes, actions and decisions
Lessons log (project log) Running record of lessons from this project and earlier ones
Lessons report Passes lessons on for others to use
Checkpoint report Team manager to project manager: one work package, at the agreed interval
Highlight report Project manager to board: stage progress and forecast, at the agreed interval
End stage report Project manager to board at a stage end: results, the case, the risks, the next stage
Exception report Project manager to board when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: cause, options, recommendation
End project report Project manager to board: performance against the PID and the business case
Digital and data management approach (PID) How data and digital tools are used, shared and protected
Exam tip

. A checkpoint report goes from the team manager to the project manager. Highlight, end stage, exception and end project reports go from the project manager to the board. A team manager who reports to the board breaks the reporting line.

3Roles and areas of focus

The roles follow the levels of management. Learn each focus, and check the Official Book's table for the exact wording.

Role Focus in the progress practice
Executive Uses reports and forecasts to confirm the project is still justified
Senior user and senior supplier Review progress for their own interest: user readiness, supplier delivery
Project manager Monitors the stage; keeps the logs; writes highlight, end stage and exception reports; forecasts and escalates
Team manager Agrees work package tolerances; sends checkpoint reports; escalates to the project manager
Project assurance Independently checks that progress information is reliable
Project support Runs the reporting tools and keeps the logs and data tidy

4Effective management and techniques

Exam tip

. Each level sets tolerances for the level below. The board sets stage tolerances; the project manager sets work package tolerances.

Tolerances can cover time, cost, quality, scope, benefits, risk and sustainability, not only time and cost.

Level Tolerance and control
Corporate or programme Sets the project tolerances; receives escalation if the board forecasts a breach
Project board Sets the stage tolerances; reads highlight reports; decides on exception reports
Project manager Sets work package tolerances; controls the stage day to day; escalates exceptions
Team manager Works within the work package tolerances; sends checkpoint reports

A good approach uses time-driven and event-driven controls together.

Type Board level Project manager level
Time-driven Highlight reports at the agreed interval Checkpoint reports; regular review of logs and registers
Event-driven Stage decisions, ad hoc direction, exception reports Authorizing and accepting work packages; escalating events
  • Review and report. Compare actual with plan, products first, at an interval that fits the stage's length and risk.
  • Forecast. Estimate where time, cost and benefits will end up, and report the trend.
  • Escalate. When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, send an exception report at once, with cause, options and a recommendation.
  • Learn. Record lessons as they appear and review them at each stage end.
  • Use data well. Keep one protected source of progress data, as the digital and data management approach sets out.
Exam tip

. When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, the project manager escalates at once. The project manager does not decide alone and does not wait for the next report. The board then decides, for example by asking for an exception plan.

5Judging a progress approach

What an effective approach looks like Red flag, with the principle
Report interval fits the stage and its risk One fixed interval for every stage (manage by stages)
Right detail: team detail to the project manager, summary and forecast to the board The board receives team-level detail (define roles)
Tolerances set at each level and used in reports No stage tolerance, or never mentioned (manage by exception)
Forecasts with trends and the effect on the case Reports only what is done; problems found at stage end (business justification)
Exceptions escalated early with options A forecast breach hidden or held for the next report (manage by exception)
Lessons captured continuously Lessons gathered only at the end (learn from experience)
Progress measured by products Progress measured by effort or time elapsed (focus on products)
Data and tools agreed and protected Inconsistent spreadsheets; sensitive data shared freely

Tailoring changes the form of progress control, never the need for it.

Setting How progress control changes
Agile team Task boards, stand-ups and iteration reviews can serve as checkpoint information if the work package agrees; the project manager still forecasts to the board
Small project Short, informal reports and fewer events; the board keeps its decision points and tolerances
Large or multi-supplier project Common templates; supplier reporting written into contracts
Sustainability, digital and data concerns Sustainability measures and data protection added to tolerances and reports
Exam tip

. A tailored approach still forecasts, sets tolerances and escalates exceptions. If an option drops one of these because the project is small or agile, it is not tailoring.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1In the build stage of Project Harbor, the stage cost tolerance is plus or minus 10 percent. Sam Okafor, the project manager, forecasts cost 14 percent over and sends an exception report to the board that day. Was this an appropriate action, and why?

  • AYes, because a forecast breach of stage tolerance should reach the board immediately
  • BYes, because the executive has to be told about every forecast variance in the stage
  • CNo, because Sam should wait for the next highlight report before showing the new figures
  • DNo, because Sam can use the project tolerance to absorb the overrun without telling the board
Show the answer

Answer: A. A forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception that must be escalated at once; the project tolerance is not Sam's to use.

S2On Project Harbor, Sam has recorded no lessons during the build stage because the team is busy. He plans to collect them all for the end project report. Was this an appropriate approach, and why?

  • AYes, because lessons only become reliable once the whole project has been delivered and closed
  • BYes, because the end project report is the only product in which lessons are recorded
  • CNo, because lessons belong in the lessons log as they appear and are reviewed each stage
  • DNo, because lessons belong in the issue register so that the change authority can act on them
Show the answer

Answer: C. Learn from experience means capturing lessons continuously in the lessons log and reviewing them at stage ends, not leaving them to the end.

S3Sam is about to authorize a work package for Wei Chen's development team on Project Harbor. Who sets the tolerances for this work package?

  • AMarta Quinn, the executive, as the person accountable for the project
  • BSam Okafor, the project manager, within the stage tolerances
  • CTomas Reyes, the senior user, as the person who accepts the products
  • DAisha Bello, project assurance, as the person who checks progress
Show the answer

Answer: B. Each level sets tolerances for the level below, so the project manager sets work package tolerances inside the stage tolerances set by the board.

S4Project Harbor's build stage lasts four months and carries a high delivery risk. Sam sends highlight reports monthly, and the board saw a slip only at the stage end. What should Sam do?

  • AAsk Wei Chen to send checkpoint reports straight to the board every week
  • BReplace the monthly highlight reports with an end stage report each month
  • CWiden the stage tolerance so that a slip of that size would fall inside it
  • DAgree a shorter highlight report interval and add forecasts to each report
Show the answer

Answer: D. The interval should fit the stage's length and risk and a forecast lets the board act early, while checkpoint reports go to the project manager.

S5Wei Chen's team works in two-week iterations with a visible task board and daily stand-ups. Sam asked for weekly written checkpoint reports, and the team says the board already shows progress. What should Sam do?

  • AAgree in the work package that the task board and stand-ups serve as checkpoint information
  • BInsist on written weekly checkpoint reports because the method allows no other format
  • CAsk the team to send highlight reports to the board each week instead of checkpoint reports
  • DRemove the work package tolerances because an iterative team cannot forecast its own progress
Show the answer

Answer: A. Tailoring may change the form of checkpoint information as long as the reporting need and the tolerances stay in place.

S6Jon Park, project support, asks which management product should state the tools that hold Project Harbor's progress data, who may see the data and how it is protected. Which product should he use?

  • AThe communication management approach in the PID
  • BThe digital and data management approach in the PID
  • CThe daily log of informal notes in the project log
  • DThe quality management approach held in the PID
Show the answer

Answer: B. The digital and data management approach covers tools, access and protection of project data, while the communication approach covers who is told what.

6.2 Recall questions

R1What is an exception?

Show the answer

A situation where a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

R2Who sends a checkpoint report, and who receives it?

Show the answer

The team manager sends it to the project manager.

R3Name the two types of control and give one example of each.

Show the answer

Time-driven, such as the highlight report; event-driven, such as the exception report.

R4Who sets the stage tolerances?

Show the answer

The project board, for the project manager.

R5What does the daily log hold?

Show the answer

The project manager's informal notes, actions and decisions not held in other products.

R6Which report reviews the whole project against the PID and the business case?

Show the answer

The end project report.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Purpose monitor, forecast and control deviations
Tolerance levels corporate sets project, board sets stage, project manager sets work package
Controls time-driven and event-driven, used together
Reports checkpoint to the project manager; highlight, end stage, exception and end project to the board
Escalation at once, when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
Effective approach right interval, forecasts, tolerances used, early escalation, continuous lessons
Tailoring change the form, keep forecasting, tolerances and escalation
